newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - BELGIAN EMU PLAN GETS GOOD MARKS FROM EU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BELGIAN EMU PLAN GETS GOOD MARKS FROM EU.

text.p: Belgium's efforts to get its budgetary house in order for economic and monetary union (EMU) got a seal of approval from its European Union partners on Monday.

European Union finance ministers said a plan to further reduce the country's deficit and debt mountain by 2000 would add to "considerable progress" already made to meeting the Maastricht Treaty criteria.

"The council carried out an examination of the new Belgian convergence programme for the period 1997-2000. It welcomed the programme's strategy for budgetary consolidation as credible, adequate to the particular public finance conditions of Belgium," the ministers said in a statement following their regular monthly ECOFIN meeting.

The plan aims to cut the state deficit from 3.4 percent in 1996 to 2.9 percent in 1997 and 1.4 percent in the year 2000 in the most cautious of three economic scenarios. The ratio of debt to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is targeted to fall from 130.4 percent in 1996 to 127.0 percent in 1997 and 120.4 pct in 2000.
The Council said it noted with satisfaction that Belgian policies in the framework of the first convergence programme (1992-1996) led to considerable progress towards meeting the EMU criteria.

But it also urged Belgium to take every opportunity to make maximum progress in reducing its debt to GDP ratio. Despite the improvement in the past years, Belgium's debt/GDP ratio is still the worst in the 15-nation bloc.

Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt, in a speech to the ECOFIN council, said Belgium's ratio of state debt to gross domestic product was set to fall by six to 10 percentage points between 1998 and 2000.
The Maastricht Treaty on EMU sets a goal of 60 percent for the debt/GDP ratio and that higher ratios might be allowed provided there is a decline to that level "at a satisfactory pace".
Maystadt said that he expected Belgium to be among the first group of countries to join the single currency in 1999.
He said his colleagues had expressed some worry about the overshoot in Belgium's health spending budget, but vowed the Belgian government would keep spending in check.

"There has been a decision to put the health sector under permanent monitoring. The government will make an evaluation of the situation in the sector every month and will take the necessary measures to meet the (budgetary) norms of the government agreement," he said.
At the end of last year, Belgium took an extra 20 billion Belgian francs of austerity measures in the health sector, following reports of a budget overshoot.
Maystadt also said that the series of scandals surrounding one of the four partners in Belgium's centre-left coalition did not prevent the government from functioning properly.
